summary:
Our team, Superstars, built Left Behind — Every machine has a story, a bilingual (English/Portuguese) interactive website about the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars. It presents 21 machines with full stories across two worlds, from Apollo 11’s Eagle in 1969 to Perseverance and Ingenuity today. Visitors can spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars to find each landing site, rover and instrument where it really is. They can also follow a timeline of milestones, hear audio narration of the stories, read “Did you know?” facts and take a ten-question quiz. Each story states how the machine’s mission ended, such as left by design, communication lost, or still operational. Every fact is traced to a source, and images are labeled as illustrations or computer-generated.

The project answers the challenge by treating discarded equipment as evidence of missions, engineering and discoveries, not as junk. It matters because it shows exploration as a chain: each machine, working or silent, made the next one possible.
details:
LEFT BEHIND - THE STORIES OF SPACE EXPLORATION

Discover the Forgotten Machines. Explore Their Stories. Uncover Their Legacy.

What it does. Left Behind turns equipment that is usually seen as abandoned into stories people want to read. Each of the 21 machines is told in seven chapters, from meeting the explorer to its legacy. A “Deep science” switch adds technical depth for advanced readers. The Atlas has 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, with filters for equipment type, mission, period and status. The site also has a timeline, a gallery, “Did you know?” facts and a ten-question quiz. In Explorer Mission, a game, players walk to real sites, search for clues and investigate hardware to unlock science briefings. Their progress saves on their device.

Benefits and impact. We want students and curious visitors to see each object as a mission, an engineering achievement and a scientific discovery. The site is built to be trustworthy and accessible. Every fact links to a source, such as NASA mission archives. Every image is labeled as an illustration, a computer-generated view or a real photograph. Every status separates a completed mission from a failure. Narrated stories, keyboard controls, a skip-to-content link and two languages help more people take part, including Portuguese speakers. We hope visitors leave understanding that exploration builds on every machine before it.

Tools. The site is a single-page web app made with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks. It uses canvas graphics for the globes and the game, separate data files for Moon and Mars machines, a translation script for English and Portuguese, and an audio-accessibility module. It is hosted on Netlify. We researched the stories using NASA’s public mission archives.

Creativity. Visitors can read, listen, explore or play, so one project suits different learning styles. We gave each machine its own ending, because “abandoned” is not one story.

What we considered. Our main concerns were scientific accuracy, honesty about what is real and what is generated, accessibility, and a language that fits our own community. Our team is six students aged 15–16 from Escola Integrada Educativa.
